notes: Chapter title. 'CAPVT SECVNDVM.' = 'CHAPTER II.' Body-region line on both sides.
Chapter subtitle. 'De ſtatu primæ quæſtionis.' = 'CONCERNING THE STATE OF THE FIRST QUESTION.'

Definition of canonical. 'LIbri autem ſacræ Scripturæ dicuntur Canonici, quia fidei noſtræ morumq́; normam & regulam continent.' = 'THE books of scripture are called canonical, because they contain the standard and rule of our faith and morals.' Latin l0027 ends mid-line at 'continent.'; rest belongs to u004.

Aristotle Politics analogy. 'Eſt enim Scriptura idem in Eccleſia, quod eſt in Republica lex, quam Ariſtoteles in Politicis, libro 2.cap. 8. κανόνα, regulam vocat.' = 'For the scripture is in the church what the law is in a state, which Aristotle in his Politics calls a canon or rule.' Greek κανόνα is paraphrased in Latin by 'regulam'; Parker collapses both into 'a canon or rule'.

Citizens and Christians analogy. 'Quemadmodum enim ciues omnes legibus publicis conuenienter viuere ac πολιτεύεσθαι; ſic Chriſtiani fidem vitamq́ue ſuam ad Scripturæ regulam, legemq́ue accommodare debẽt.' = 'As all citizens are bound to live and behave agreeably to the public laws, so Christians should square their faith and conduct by the rule and law of scripture.' Greek πολιτεύεσθαι has no Latin paraphrase; Parker absorbs its meaning into 'behave agreeably to the public laws'. Sentence crosses p0032/p0033 page boundary.

Paul of Samosata accusation. 'Itaq; apud Euſebium,lib. 7.cap. 30. ſancti Patres Paulum Samoſatenum accuſant, quòd ἀποςὰς τῡ κανόνος, à regula discedens, hæretici dogmatis author extitiſſet.' = 'So, in Eusebius, the holy fathers accuse Paul of Samosata of departing from the rule (ἀποστὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ κανόνος), and becoming the author of an heretical opinion.' Latin paraphrase 'à regula discedens' collapsed; Parker preserves Greek in parens with the modern accentuated form (Parker spelling ἀπὸ τοῦ vs. Whitaker τῡ).

Tertullian + Cyprian patristic citations. 'Eiuſmodi eſt quod Tertullianus in lib. aduerſ. Hermogenem, Scripturas appellat regulam veritatis: & Cyprianus ait in ſermone de Baptiſmo Chriſti, Inueniet ex hac Scriptura omnium doctrinarum regulas emanaſſe: & hinc naſci, & huc reuerti quicquid Eccleſiaſtica continet disciplina.' = 'So Tertullian, in his book against Hermogenes, calls the scripture the rule of faith; and Cyprian says, in his discourse upon the baptism of Christ: "One will find that the rules of all doctrine are derived from this scripture; and that, whatever the discipline of the church contains springs hence, and returns hither."'

Chrysostom homily citation. '& Chryſoſt. homil. 13. in 2. Corinth. Scripturam vocat ἁπάντων ἀκριβῆ ζυγὸν, καὶ γνώμονα, καὶ κανόνα, exquisitam omnium rerum trutinam, & normam, & regulam.' = 'Chrysostom too, in his 13th Homily upon 2 Corinthians calls scripture the exact balance, and standard, and rule of all things.' Greek + Latin paraphrase pair (the Latin 'exquisitam omnium rerum trutinam, & normam, & regulam' translates the immediately-preceding Greek); Parker drops the Greek and renders the meaning once. Sentence crosses p0043/p0044 page boundary in Parker.

Augustine: de doctrina Christiana + Scripturas-as-scales (contra Donatistas). 'Ob iſtam cauſam Auguſtinus ait, de doctrina Chriſtiana lib. 2. cap. 8. in Scripturis inueniri omnia, quæ continent fidem, moresqúe viuendi: & Scripturas ſtatêram vocat, lib. 2. cap. 6. contra Donatiſtas, his verbis: Afferamus non ſtatêras doloſas, vbi expendamus quod volumus, & quomodo volumus, ſed afferamus diuinas ſtatêras de Scripturis ſanctis, &c.' = 'For the same reason Augustine affirms, that "whatever belongs to faith and moral life may be found in the scriptures;" and he calls the scripture the scales, in the following passage: "Let us not apply deceitful scales, where we may weigh what we wish, and as we wish; but let us bring God\u2019s own scales from the holy scriptures," &c.'

Basil + Ruffinus citations. 'Sic Baſilius ſacram doctrinam appellat κανόνα ἀὐϑέος, καὶ γνώμονα ἀληϑείας, canonem recti, normamqúe veri, cui nihil omnino deſit. Et Ruffinus, poſtquam ſacros Scripturæ libros recenſuiſſet, in expoſitione Symboli, Hæc ſunt (inquit) quæ Patres intra Canonem concluſerunt, ex quibus fidei noſtræ aſſertiones conſtare voluerunt: & ſtatim, Ex his fontibus verbi diuini hauriẽda ſunt pocula.' = 'So Basil calls the sacred doctrine "the canon of rectitude and rule of truth," which fails in no part of perfection: and Ruffinus, in his exposition of the creed, after enumerating the books of scripture, adds, "These are the books which the fathers included in the canon, and from which they willed that the assertions of our faith should be demonstrated;" and then he subjoins: "From these fountains of the divine word our cups are to be drawn."' Greek + Latin paraphrase pair for Basil (κανόνα... = canonem recti, normamqúe veri); Parker collapses to English only.

Aquinas citation. 'Et Aquinas, 1. Tim. 6. Lect. 1. Doctrina (inquit) Apoſtolorum & Prophetarum Canonica dicitur, quia est quaſiregula intellectus noſtri.' = 'Aquinas too lays down, that "the doctrine of the apostles and prophets is called canonical, because it is, as it were, the rule of our intellect."'

Synthesis: why scripture is canonical. 'Hinc quamobrem Scripturæ dicantur Canonica, perſpicuum eſt, quia quid nos credere, & quemadmodum viuere oporteat, præſcribunt, vt huc fidem omnem, vitamq́ue noſtram referamus, quemadmodum lapicida aut architectus ad amuſſim & perpendiculum opus ſuum exigit.' = 'Hence it plainly appears why the scriptures are called canonical;\u2014because they prescribe to us what we must believe, and how we ought to live: so that we should refer to this test our whole faith and life, as the mason or architect squares his work by the line and plummet.' Note 'perſpicuum eſt' = 'plainly appears' (NOT 'perspicuous' — this is the ordinary, not the doctrinal-technical, sense).

Forward-reference to Q VI on perfection. 'Ex quo etiam animaduerti poteſt, perfectam eſſe Scripturam : nam aliter nomen hoc Canonis & Regulæ Scripturis non ſatis idoneè conueniret : qua de re in ſexta quæſtione dicendum erit.' = 'Hence, too, we may perceive that the scripture is perfect, since otherwise the title of canon or rule could hardly be applied to it; upon which point we shall have to speak under the sixth question.' Sentence crosses p0033/p0034 page boundary.

OT/NT books called Testamentary. 'Hi autem libri, qui Canonici vocantur, in vetere nouoóque Teſtamento comprehenduntur, ideoóque Teſtamentarii nuncupantur.' = 'Now these books, which are called canonical, are comprised in the old and new Testaments, and are therefore styled Testamentary.'

Eusebius / Nicephorus Greek terminology. 'Sic Euſebius, libro tertio capite tertio, hos libros vocat ἐνδιαθήκους, eodemq́ue vocabulo Nicephorus ſæpe vſus eſt, aliiq́ue Græci ſcriptores: ſunt etiam qui διαθηκογράφους vocent.' = 'So Eusebius calls these books ἐνδιαθήκους; and Nicephorus often uses the same term. Some also call them διαθηκογράφους.' No Latin paraphrase for either Greek term; Parker preserves both Greek words verbatim. Sentence crosses p0044/p0045 page boundary in Parker.

Statement of the controversy. 'Iam ergo inter nos & Papiſtas quæritur, quinam libri ſint verè κανονικοὶ καὶ ἐνδιάθηκοι.' = 'The question, then, between us and the papists is, What books are to be esteemed canonical and testamentary.' Greek κανονικοὶ καὶ ἐνδιάθηκοι has no Latin paraphrase but Parker DROPS the Greek entirely and renders the meaning ('canonical and testamentary') — unusual; contrast u015 where Parker preserved the same root verbatim. Possible reason: u016 is the headline sentence, where English clarity outranks Greek-preservation.

Areas of agreement / disagreement. 'De multis & præcipuis conſtat atque conuenit: de quibuſdam litigatur.' = 'Concerning many, and indeed the principal ones, we are agreed: concerning some we are at variance.'

Programmatic move to Trent. 'Vt huius autem quæſtionis verus ſtatus intelligi poſſit, videndum eſt inprimis, quid hac de re Tridentinum Cócilium decreuerit.' = 'But, in order that the true state of this question may be understood, we must see, in the first place, what the council of Trent hath determined upon this subject.' Note Parker uses 'hath' (Rule 2a register).

Trent Session 4 decree text — preamble. 'Concilii hæc verba ſunt, Seſſ. 4. Sacrorum librorum indicem huic decreto aſcribendum cenſuit, ne cui dubitatio ſuboriri poſsit, quinam ab ipſa Synodo ſuſcipiuntur.' = 'Its words are as follows: "The synod hath deemed it fitting that a catalogue of the sacred books should be subjoined to this decree, lest any should have occasion to doubt what books are received by it."' Parker uses 'hath' again.

Trent recites the canonical. 'Tum recitat libros, qui verè Canonici ſunt, quiq́ue à nobis ſine vlla dubitatione ſuſcipiuntur.' = 'Then it recites the books which are truly canonical, and are received by us without any hesitation.'
Trent adds the disputed. 'Deinde alios adiungit, quos pro verè Canonicis non agnoſcimus.' = 'But it subjoins others which we do not acknowledge as canonical.'

The disputed six. 'Eiuſmodi ſunt hi ſex libri, Tobias, Iudith, Sapientia, Eccleſiaſticus, Maccabæorum duo.' = 'Such are these six books: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, two books of Maccabees.' Note: 'Maccabæorum duo' = 1 + 2 Maccabees, making six total (Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, 1 Macc, 2 Macc).

Closing tag for OT list. 'Hi ſunt libri veteris Teſtamenti.' = 'These are the books of the old Testament.' Parker compresses the boundary: 'These are the books of the old Testament. Afterwards,' on one line (l0014).

NT books — accepted uncontested though not always uniformly received. 'Pòſt recenſet libros noui Teſtamenti, quos omnes ſine controuerſia recipimus, etſi non ſemper omnes ſimiliter recepti fuerunt in Eccleſia, vt poſtea audietis.' = 'Afterwards, it enumerates the books of the new Testament, all of which we receive without any controversy, although they were not always alike received in the church, as you shall hear in the sequel.'

Trent's anathema clause. 'Concludit poſtremò Concilium in hanc ſententiam: Si quis libros ipſos integros cum omnibus ſuis partibus, vt in vetere vulgata Latina editione habentur, pro ſacris & Canonicis non ſuſceperit, anathema ſit.' = 'Finally, the council concludes in these words: "Whoever does not receive these books entire with all their parts, as they are contained in the ancient Latin Vulgate, for sacred and canonical, let him be accursed!"'
Summary tag for the decree. 'Habetis decretum Tridentinum, & decreti terribilem ſanctionem.' = 'Here you have the decree of the Tridentine council, and the terrible sanction of that decree.'

Long sentence enumerating what Trent demands be received: six books plus deuterocanonical additions (Baruch, Hymn of the Three Children, Susannah, Bel and the Dragon, apocryphal Esther chapters). 'Ex his nunc manifeſtum eſt iuberi nos à Tridentinis Patribus, ſi modò diras iſtas effugere volumus, vt non modò ſex illos integros libros, quos nominaui, ſed præterea etiam partes illas, & additamenta librorum, cuiuſmodi ſunt, Baruch, Hymnus trium puerorum, Suſannæ, Belis, & Draconis hiſtoriæ, quæ Danieli tribuuntur, Heſteræ capita quædam apocrypha, in Canonicæ Scripturæ authoritatem recipiamus.' = 'From these premises it now appears that we are required by the Tridentine fathers, if we would escape their anathema, to receive as authoritative canonical scripture not only those six entire books which we have mentioned, but besides certain parts of and additions to the books, as Baruch, the Hymn of the three Children, the histories of Susannah and Bel and the Dragon, which are attributed to Daniel, and certain apocryphal chapters of the book of Esther:' Sentence crosses p0034/p0035 page boundary.

Jesuit interpretation tag. 'Sic enim huius decreti ſententiam interpretantur Ieſuitæ.' = 'for it is thus that the Jesuits interpret the meaning of this decree.' Parker treats this as a trailing clause to u027 in punctuation (no capital after the colon), but it's a complete subordinate sentence in the Latin.

Formal restatement of the question. 'Eſt ergo ſtatus huius quæſtionis, Vtrum hi libri,& hę librorũ particulę pro ſacra & Canonica Scriptura recipi debeant.' = 'Now, therefore, the state of the question is this; whether these books, and these parts of books, should be received for sacred and canonical scriptures?'

Bare antithesis. 'Illi ſtatuunt: Nos negamus.' = 'They affirm: we deny.' Both Latin l0012 and Parker l0033 are shared across THREE consecutive units (u029, u030, u031) because the line packs three short sentences.
Transition to disputation proper. 'Sequitur iam vt ad ipſam diſceptationem veniamus.' = 'It remains that we should proceed to the discussion.'

Method statement (refute then defend; Aristotle's practice). 'Et primùm illorum argumentis reſpondebo, tum ad noſtræ cauſæ defenſionem accedam, quam viam poſtea etiam ſequar, quia hanc noſtræ tractationi accommodatiſſimam eſſe iudico, eaque Ariſtotelem ferè vſum eſſe video.' = 'I will first answer their arguments, and then proceed to the defence of our cause; which course I intend to follow throughout, because I deem it most suitable to the matter we have in hand, and I perceive that it hath been generally adopted by Aristotle.' Authorial 'I' (Rule 7a) — first-person singulars 'iudico', 'video'. Sentence crosses p0045/p0046 page boundary in Parker.

Closing Nazianzen citation + program statement. 'Nazianzenus ait in Lib. 1. Theologiæ, Διττῶ ὄντος λόγȣ παντὸς, τῶ μὲ τὸ ὀικεῖον κατασκευάζοντος,τῶ δὲ τὸ ἀντίπαλον ἀνατρέποντος: ego prius τὸ ἀντίπαλον, quod aduerſatur, euertam, & deinde τὸ ὀικεῖον, proprium inſtitutum, confirmabo.' = 'And since, as Nazianzen tells us, "every argument is designed either to establish our own opinion, or overturn the opposite," I will choose first to overturn the opposite opinion, and then to establish my own.' Whitaker embeds two Greek terms (τὸ ἀντίπαλον, τὸ ὀικεῖον) with adjacent Latin paraphrases ('quod aduerſatur', 'proprium inſtitutum') in his own programmatic response; Parker drops both Greek and Latin paraphrase, rendering only meaning. Final sentence of chapter 2 (next line p0035_l0023 is CAPVT TERTIVM).
